summary: Defines the scenarios in which IPv6 transition mechanisms are meant to be used in unmanaged networks, typically home or small office networks. Scenarios are specific to one subnet and described by the IP connectivity offered by the gateway and the ISP. The aim is to help evaluate which transition mechanisms suit them.

eli5.summary: Homes will switch from an old kind of internet address to a new one. This describes typical home setups so we can judge which switching tricks fit.

subtitle: How homes and small offices will transition from IPv4 to IPv6

tldr.problem: IPv6 deployment will happen unevenly: some providers and gateways will upgrade before others, creating scenarios where unmanaged networks (homes and small offices) need to operate with varying levels of IPv4 and IPv6 support from their gateway and ISP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four deployment stages based on what the gateway and ISP support: Case A (gateway has no IPv6), Case B (dual-stack gateway with dual-stack ISP), Case C (dual-stack gateway with IPv4-only ISP), and Case D (gateway with IPv6-only ISP).
tldr.outcome: Applications can be evaluated and designed to work across these scenarios, and transition mechanisms can be prioritized based on what different networks will actually need.

today: RFC 3750 is an Internet Standard describing the IPv6 transition scenarios that actually occurred in practice. Many home networks still exist in Case B or C as of 2024.

sections.title: Unmanaged Networks and IPv6 Deployment
sections.content:
Unmanaged networks are home networks or small office networks typically composed of a single subnet connected to the Internet through a gateway (possibly performing NAT and firewall functions). Unlike enterprise networks, these networks have no competent administrator; the gateway is usually a simple appliance with static policies.

The RFC focuses on single-subnet networks to develop realistic scenarios for evaluating which IPv6 transition mechanisms are needed. It examines four classes of applications: local (file and printer sharing within the home), client (web browsing, email), peer-to-peer (with external participants), and server (hosting web or email services). Each type has different requirements for IPv6 addresses, DNS naming and network connectivity.
sections.eli5: Your home is a tiny network that is not managed by anyone clever. This explains how to get IPv6 working as different parts of the system get upgraded at different times.

sections.title: Application Requirements for IPv6 Networks
sections.content:
Local applications require only local connectivity and can be isolated from the Internet for security. Client applications require global connectivity and a stable IPv6 address for the duration of their session, plus access to DNS. Peer-to-peer applications (between internal and external hosts) require global addresses and stable connections, with key security needs around peer identification and data integrity. Server applications require global addresses, stable addresses for DNS publication, and careful security to prevent unintended service exposure.

Privacy is a specific concern for client applications. The RFC notes that randomizing the host identifier portion of IPv6 addresses (per RFC 3041) provides limited but real benefits: it prevents correlating multiple connections from the same device and hides hardwired device identifiers. However, if the network prefix remains constant, it cannot hide which physical location a connection originates from.
sections.eli5: Different kinds of programs need different levels of stability and privacy. A web browser is different from a file-sharing program, which is different from a server.

sections.title: Case A: Host Deployment Without Gateway Support
sections.content:
In Case A, the gateway provides no IPv6, either because it has not been upgraded or because upgrading is not practical. Some hosts attempt IPv6 deployment on their own to run IPv6-only applications or improve performance. The primary focus is peer-to-peer applications, as they can be deployed in a coordinated fashion with built-in naming (not dependent on DNS).

For hosts behind a NAT, obtaining global IPv6 connectivity requires tunneling over UDP or TCP. UDP is preferred to avoid the poor performance caused by TCP timeouts and retransmissions. If servers are needed, they should be deployed as part of the application's infrastructure to keep costs manageable. Reverse DNS lookup is difficult, which may block some client applications that require it.
sections.eli5: Your gateway does not know about IPv6, so programs have to tunnel through it using tricks to get IPv6 working on their own.

sections.title: Cases B, C and D: Upgraded Gateways and Providers
sections.content:
In Case B, both the gateway and ISP are dual-stack. Hosts obtain IPv4 addresses (from the gateway), IPv6 link-local addresses, and IPv6 global addresses allocated by the ISP. Client, peer-to-peer and server applications can all be enabled easily. The RFC argues against providing IPv4-to-IPv6 translation services, as application relays are complex and network-level translation (NAT-PT) requires complementary application layer gateways.

Case C is similar to Case B but the ISP provides only IPv4. The gateway uses automatic tunnels (6to4 per RFC 3056) or configured tunnels to gain IPv6 connectivity. Case D represents the final stage where the ISP is IPv6-only. The gateway must provide IPv4-over-IPv6 tunneling so internal IPv4 hosts can reach IPv4 services. DNS services in Case D must be provisioned using IPv6 mechanisms and can reach IPv4-only nameservers through the tunnel.
sections.eli5: As gateways and ISPs upgrade, they can directly provide IPv6 addresses. When upgrades are incomplete, tunnels let the newer parts talk to the older parts.

sections.title: Security and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Security solutions in IPv6 unmanaged networks will combine firewall functions in the gateway, authentication and authorization in applications, encryption and authentication via IP Security and Transport Layer Security, and host-based security products. Local applications should be isolated from the Internet. Peer-to-peer connections should only be used by authorized peers. Tunneling protocols for IPv6 access over IPv4 must be designed securely, and infrastructure servers should not be vulnerable to abuse.

Many unmanaged networks will need to coexist with IPv4-only hosts and devices. The RFC concludes that requiring dual-stack support is both practical and robust: general-purpose systems like personal computers should be effectively dual-stack, while IPv6-only devices are acceptable only when designed for applications that do not require IPv4 interoperation.
sections.eli5: As you add IPv6, keep the security protections you already have. Devices should support both IPv4 and IPv6 unless they are made for a specific IPv6-only purpose.
